name: What to Expect from Commercial Construction Loan Draws in Los Angeles County

mainEntity.name: How do commercial construction lenders in Los Angeles County typically structure draw schedules and inspections, and what should owners expect during funding?
mainEntity.text: How do commercial construction lenders in Los Angeles County typically structure draw schedules and inspections, and what should owners expect during funding?

acceptedAnswer.text: While loan structures vary by institution, commercial construction lending in Los Angeles County commonly relies on a draw process where funds are disbursed in stages based on work completed. The owner submits a draw request with contractor billings, lien waivers, and updated budgets or schedules. The lender typically sends an inspector or third-party consultant to verify that the claimed progress matches actual work in place. Draws are often scheduled monthly, but processing can take days or weeks depending on lender procedures and documentation quality. This creates a timing gap between when the contractor expects payment and when loan funds arrive. Owners must ensure they have sufficient cash to bridge this gap so that subcontractors are paid on time and work momentum is not lost. Lenders may also impose conditions for each draw, such as maintaining contingency levels, meeting key milestones, or resolving significant change orders. Cost overruns, delays, or unapproved changes can trigger closer scrutiny or require equity infusions. Owners should discuss draw processes, inspection frequency, and expected turnaround times with potential lenders before closing the loan. Establishing clear documentation standards with the contractor and hiring an experienced construction accountant or project manager to administer draws can significantly reduce funding-related stress during construction.
acceptedAnswer.description: Commercial construction loans in Los Angeles County are usually funded through draws tied to percentage-of-completion inspections and documentation. Owners should anticipate regular site visits by lender inspectors, detailed backup for costs, and timing gaps between contractor billing and lender disbursement that require sufficient working capital.
